title: The fourth sight: a wanderer
hookLine: a shaven man in a robe, owning nothing, calm
carry: there is another way to live
last: MARANA — EVERYONE WE LOVE WILL GO.

lines: A SHAVED HEAD, A BOWL, A ROBE.
cards: A shaved head. A plain robe the color of earth. A bowl, and as far as anyone can tell, nothing else.
Three rides have brought three shocks: age, sickness, death. If the story stopped there, it would be a very sad one, and the prince might have hidden in his gardens for life.
But on a fourth ride, more troubled than he has ever been, he sees this man walking along the road. And his face is calm. Not cheerful, not grim.
Calm, in a world that just showed the prince three reasons to despair.

teach.b: Who is that, the prince asks. Channa says: a samana. A wanderer, one who has gone forth.
The word comes from a root meaning to strive, to make an effort.

The Buddha's India had many of them: men, and some women, who left home, gave up property and family life, and walked the roads seeking answers to exactly the prince's questions. Why do we age? Why do we suffer?
Is there a way out? They lived on what people put in their bowls, slept in forests and caves, and debated each other in public halls.
They weren't one group; there were many teachers and many paths. The Jains, whose tradition is still alive today, came from this same world.
So did the Buddha: for the rest of his life, outsiders would call him the samana Gotama. Here's the heart of the fourth sight.
The first three were questions. The fourth was a possibility. Age, sickness and death come for everyone, palace or no palace.
And here was someone who had looked at the same facts and was not afraid. The stories say something in the prince went still and bright. Not an answer yet.
Just the sense that there is another way to live, and someone is already living it.

teach.h: THERE IS ANOTHER WAY TO LIVE.

how: Buddhist monks and nuns today still follow the samana's way of life in many places, shaving their heads, wearing robes and receiving food as alms, and lay Buddhists often honor them as living examples of another way to live.

o: a wanderer who left home and family to seek the truth
a temple priest who performs rites for village families
a royal guard who watched the roads for the king

games.q: what's inside the fourth sight — tap the pairs.

s: samanas were all followers of one teacher
there were many wanderers and many paths. the Jains came from the same world.
outsiders later called the Buddha the samana Gotama
he became one of the wanderers himself.
the word samana comes from a root meaning to strive
a samana is one who makes an effort: a seeker.

games.q: you've just seen age, sickness and death, and now a calm man with a bowl walks by. what do you ask?
games.why: he asks who the man is. Channa tells him: a samana, one who has gone forth. and something in the prince goes still and bright.

practice: Bring to mind the calmest face you have ever seen: a teacher, a grandparent, a stranger on a train, even a statue. Notice the eyes, the mouth, the shoulders.
Then let your own face do a little of the same: soften the jaw, rest the eyes, and let calm be possible for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Samana. A wanderer, one who strives: someone who has left home to seek the truth. The fourth sight, and the first hope.

orig.note: Pali: a wanderer, an ascetic, one who strives. Sanskrit śramaṇa.

carryVoice: Your line: there is another way to live. Calm, it turns out, is possible. Four sights, all seen.

sources.ref: Mahapadana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 14): the one gone forth, the fourth sight
Samannaphala Sutta (Digha Nikaya 2): the wandering teachers of the Buddha's time
